The integrated scene shows the same: C:/dev/fable-space-game/out/screens/integration/budget-leo-cockpit.png
findings.defect: The whole cabin still reads as an untextured clay render. Ring frames, stringers, close-out panels, lockers, hatch and console are each one flat matte tone (grey or beige) with hard, unlit edges; no surface shows a highlight, a gloss change, a scratch or a fingerprint at seat distance. Parts declared metallic (aluminium ring frames and stringers, steel fasteners, handholds, the 'chrome' switch levers) look like flat grey paint or go black. The baked detail layers, edge wear and grime are invisible beyond about 0.3 m; where wear does show (hand-controller bases in look-back-couches-hatch.png) it is a sprinkle of separate white dots along the edges, not a worn edge.
findings.realReference: Apollo CM, Orion and Crew Dragon cabin photographs: painted aluminium panels with visible sheen and soft window highlights that slide across them, brushed and anodised metal with streaked highlights and coloured sheen, bright continuous wear lines on handled edges, scuffs around latches, dense placards, Velcro grids, stowage bags, cable bundles with slack. Local contrast is high: a metal frame next to a window shows the bright window and the dark console in it.
findings.likelyCause: src/render/cockpit/shaders.ts shade(): there is no reflection of the cabin for glossy and metallic surfaces. Line 833 `ambientSpec = amb.uniformE * (f0 * 0.5 + 0.02) * (1.0 - roughness) / PI` is a direction-less constant, and cabinLight() adds one representative-point lobe per window or flood only. A metallic = 1 material therefore has no diffuse and a flat specular: uniform grey (aluminium 0.91) or black (steel levers). Half of the diffuse light is the direction-less integrating-sphere term `amb.uniformE * occ.ao * cavity` (line 834), so the detail normal maps (detailStrength 0.5-0.8 in data/defs/visuals/cockpits/kestrel.json) shade nothing. Wear: materialDetail line 682 thresholds a noise texture (`smoothstep(1 - mat.d.y, ..., tM.b)`) on FLAG_EDGE chamfers, so with wear.amount 0.12-0.3 only isolated noise peaks pass, which gives dots. The detail set is 8 procedural 512^2 layers; none of the 50 USD texture budget was spent.
findings.fixDirection: 1) Give the cabin a specular environment: render the interior into a small cube map (128-256^2, from the cabin centre and re-rendered when the sun, floods or attitude change, prefiltered mips, parallax-corrected to the cone) and use it for every interior material's specular and for the glass reflections; this alone makes metals, paint sheen and switch levers read. 2) Replace the constant uniformE with a directional ambient (SH or per-vertex bent normal with the window, patch and flood polygons) so normals and detail maps shade. 3) Drive edge wear from distance to the edge with low-frequency breakup (continuous bright line, wider at corners), not from a thresholded noise. 4) Replace the procedural detail layers with photographed or generated PBR sets for painted aluminium, anodise, beta cloth and Nomex at higher contrast, and add the missing clutter (stowage bags, cable slack, tape, placard density). Re-shoot every seat view and compare side by side with an Orion or Apollo cabin photograph.

findings.defect: The insulation blankets, which fill most of every seat view, are flat-topped boxes with a hard bevel (each bay shows a lighter rectangle inside a darker one with straight facet edges) and a diamond grid of wide, soft, dark lines drawn on the flat face. There is no relief: no cell bulges, nothing pinches at the seams, no wrinkle or sag. In night-displays-floods.png the lines bend and stretch across the bays like a warped projection. It reads as a line pattern on cardboard, not as quilted cloth.
findings.realReference: Quilted or tufted spacecraft liners (Soyuz orbital module, Shuttle middeck and payload-bay blankets, beta-cloth covers): every cell is a small pillow with its own shading gradient, the seam is a thread line 1-2 mm wide sitting in a crease, the cloth wrinkles toward tie-downs and sags between them, and the weave has a soft sheen. More often still the liner is smooth fabric with snaps, Velcro and labels.
findings.likelyCause: src/render/cockpit/cabin/shell.ts blanket() (lines 437-453): one patch on a 4 cm grid with the profile `edge(x) = min(1, d * 6) ** 0.5`, i.e. a plateau with a ramp only in the outer 8 percent, resolved by one or two grid cells: a bevelled box. The quilting exists only in shaders.ts materialDetail case 1 (lines 686-707): a slope of 0.22 that the direction-less cabin light does not shade, plus `d.cavity *= mix(0.7, 1.0, puff)` and `d.grime = max(d.grime, (1.0 - puff) * 0.6)` over `smoothstep(0.0, 0.11 * fill, seam)`, which paints a dark band about 15 mm wide along every seam.
findings.fixDirection: Model the relief: tessellate blankets to about 1 cm at lod0 (135 k triangles of the budget are unused) and displace per quilt cell (pillow profile per diamond, pinched at seams and tufts) plus low-frequency sag and wrinkle noise, with the occlusion bake picking up the creases. Make the seam a 1-2 mm stitch line and drop the seam grime to 0.15 or less. Shade the cloth with the cloth BRDF and a weave normal so it has sheen. Vary bays (some smooth panels with snaps and Velcro) so the wall is not one pattern.

findings.view: C:/dev/fable-space-game/out/screens/cockpit/leo-sun-patch-console.png; closeup-mfd.png; closeup-fdai.png; closeup-switches.png; perf-1440p-leo-seat.png (stale, 10 Nov, same fault)
findings.defect: The brief's 'hard sun patch on the console' has shredded edges. Along the lower-left edge of the patch, to the right of MFD 1 and around the FDAI, the boundary breaks into a comb of parallel streaks several centimetres long, all pointing along the sun's direction on the panel, like torn paper or motion smear. It is the brightest, highest-contrast feature of the hero seat view and it is visible at normal field of view, not only in the close-ups.
findings.realReference: Sunlight through a spacecraft window (Apollo CM, ISS cupola, Crew Dragon): the patch is the window's outline with a clean edge and a penumbra of about 1 cm per metre of throw, and crisp shadows of whatever stands in the beam. No streaks.
findings.likelyCause: The cabin's own sun map self-shadows the lit console face at grazing incidence. src/render/cockpit/sunmap.ts line 88-89: the caster pipeline uses `cullMode: 'none'` and no depthBias or depthBiasSlopeScale, and the console face that receives the patch is itself a caster (feature.ts line 567: casters are the drawn detail level minus the enclosure). In shaders.ts sunMapVisibility() the bias is at most 3.5 texels of depth plus a 3.5 texel normal offset (lines 516-517), while at the 10-15 degree sun elevation of this view one 2 mm texel spans 8-12 mm of depth. Away from any occluder the blocker search finds nothing and returns 1 (line 531), so the patch interior is clean; within the search radius of a real shadow edge (14 texels, stretched to 10-20 cm on the panel at this angle) the 8 x 8 PCF runs and compares neighbouring texels of the receiver's own plane against one reference depth, which gives the streaks.
findings.fixDirection: Remove the receiver's self-occlusion instead of tuning constants: draw the sun map with front faces culled (closed console and bezel boxes then cast from their back faces only), or add `depthBiasSlopeScale` to the sun-map pipeline, and make the shader bias proportional to the tangent of the incidence (clamped). Compute the receiver-plane slope `dzduv` analytically from the geometric normal and the sun-map axes rather than from screen derivatives. Add a browser test that puts the sun at 8, 15 and 30 degrees to the console face and asserts the lit fraction is monotonic across the patch edge along three scan lines.

findings.defect: What is seen through the windows is placeholder. moon-horizon.png: the Moon is a featureless pale-grey area cut from black by one perfectly straight line. leo-earth-side-window.png: the Earth is a washed-out pale-blue smear with a ruler-straight white band for the limb, no cloud, coast or ocean, and the cabin around it is black. chase-window-sun.png: a plain grey cone against a flat blue gradient with a black hole for the window and no reflection in the glass. pad-noon-forward-window.png: white-blue fog outside, no sky, tower or cloud. These are four of the brief's reviewed acceptance views and each is exactly what PROMPT.txt bans (blue gradients, smooth spheres, placeholder art).
findings.realReference: Apollo LM window photographs (cratered, sharply shadowed regolith to a curved, uneven horizon), ISS and Apollo photographs of Earth through a window (cloud systems, coastlines, a thin layered blue limb, the window frame as a dark silhouette with rim light), exterior photographs of Dragon and Orion windows (Earth and sky mirrored in the glass, sun glints, lit bezel and shade inside).
findings.likelyCause: Lab stand-ins, not the cockpit's shaders: C:/dev/fable-space-game/labs/cockpit/main.ts line 235 builds the scene from createLabPlanetFeature() (low-resolution albedo sphere), createLabSkyFeature() and createLabHullFeature() (labs/cockpit/hull.ts, one material 'backshell' [0.72, 0.73, 0.72]); hand-off deviation 7 says so. Consequence: there is no reviewed evidence that any window view of the brief works with the real Earth, Moon, atmosphere, pad or capsule exterior, and the exposure compensation chosen for the stand-ins (ec=-3, ec=-2 in tests/browser/cockpit/views.spec.ts) leaves the cabin black and the subject pale.
findings.fixDirection: Shoot the window views where the real world exists: labs/integration draws the cockpit since commit 346aa55. Add the pad, LEO Earth, Moon horizon, reentry and both chase views there (a spec under tests/browser/cockpit that opens the integration lab with the seat camera, or a request to the integration owner), look at them, and fix what the real scene shows. Expose each like a photographer would: for Earth or the Moon expose for the subject and let the window frame go to a dark silhouette with rim light; for the cabin let the window clip. Keep the stand-in lab for functional tests only and stop presenting its frames as the acceptance screenshots.

findings.defect: The frame is 98 percent black and the screenshot spec now fails on it (`chase-window-night: mostly black (0.019)`, tests/browser/cockpit/views.spec.ts:57; the other 18 functional tests pass). Two dim window shapes float in a void: the hull has no silhouette at all, there are no stars and no Earth night side, and the lit cabin behind the glass is barely above black apart from one flood lens.
findings.realReference: A lit crewed capsule on the night side (Crew Dragon and Soyuz filmed from the ISS): the windows glow clearly, warm or cool by lamp type, and are the brightest thing in frame; the hull is faintly readable from window spill, earthshine or moonlight, against stars and city lights.
findings.likelyCause: Regression from outside the package after the screenshots were last taken: render-core commit aa8fd79 ('a lit area brighter than the prior sets the exposure from 2 % of the frame', src/render/core/post/exposure.ts, 10 Nov 21:46). The directly visible flood lens now sets the exposure and the shot's `ec=-2` (views.spec.ts line 46) pushes the cabin under black. Independently, nothing in the lab lights or outlines the hull at night.
findings.fixDirection: Re-tune the shot for the new metering (drop ec to 0 or frame so no bare lamp is in view), then check the same view in the integration lab with the real exterior, stars and Earth night side. From outside, the cabin should be exposed so the windows read as lit rooms; if the core's highlight rule under-exposes interiors seen through glass, file a request against the exposure governor rather than compensating per shot.

findings.defect: Cabin light has no direction, falloff or cast shadow, and every scene is exposed to the same brightness. The 'night side lit only by displays and floodlights' view looks like an evenly lit office at noon: no pool of light under a flood, no dark corner, no shadow from the console, ring frames or handholds, no blue glow from the displays on the panel around them. On the pad the wall beside a window is no brighter than the far wall. The 4.5 cm deep ring frames cast nothing onto the blankets in any view.
findings.realReference: Apollo, Shuttle and Orion night-pass photographs: a few lamps make bright pools with fast falloff, the rest of the cabin sinks into shadow, displays tint nearby surfaces, and the picture is low-key overall. By day the surfaces next to a window are several stops brighter than those across the cabin, with soft shadows behind every frame.
findings.likelyCause: shaders.ts line 834: the integrating-sphere term `amb.uniformE * occ.ao * cavity` (kestrel.json lighting.cabinAlbedo 0.5 makes it equal to the mean direct irradiance) fills everything evenly. Floods are occluded by one baked scalar for all six lamps together (`occ.flood`, lumen-weighted, occlusion.ts), stored per vertex at 3.5 cm spacing, so no lamp casts a shadow of its own; windows use one radiance and per-vertex visibility. Exposure: the core's interior metering adapts fully to the cabin mean, so a 5 cd/m^2 night cabin is displayed like a 500 cd/m^2 one.
findings.fixDirection: Give each flood its own visibility (the six lamps are static: one small shadow map or one baked channel per lamp) and shade them as the directional sources they are; cut the uniform term to the true second bounce (bake first-bounce irradiance per vertex per source instead). Let display glow show: it needs the lower exposure. Ask the core for a luminance-dependent key for interior cameras (about -1.5 EV when the adapted mean is under 10 cd/m^2) so night looks like night, or publish an exposure hint from the cockpit.

findings.defect: At night the windows are uniform mid-grey rectangles (sampled 112,112,112 and 107,108,107 across both panes). They read as opaque grey shades or missing textures, not as glass onto black space.
findings.realReference: A cabin window at night is a dark mirror: black outside with stars or city lights, and over it a recognisable reflected image of the lit cabin, with the displays as bright rectangles, doubled by the two panes.
findings.likelyCause: shaders.ts cabinRadianceAlong() line 1092: `var L = amb.uniformE * cabin.bounce.w / PI * 1.6` is returned for every reflected ray that does not hit a display, flood or sun-patch polygon, and glass() adds it at `2.0 * F` per pane for two panes: about 13 percent of the cabin's mean luminance as a flat value. With the exposure adapted to the cabin that is 40 percent display grey.
findings.fixDirection: Reflect an image, not a constant: sample the cabin reflection cube proposed in the first finding (parallax-corrected) along the reflected ray, keep the exact display and flood hits on top, and offset the second pane's reflection. Verify against black space that the window shows stars through a faint cabin reflection.

findings.defect: The reentry view is the pad view with a sepia filter. Both windows are featureless pure white with a faint salmon fringe, and every surface in the cabin has the same flat salmon tone; there is no gradient from the windows, no flicker structure, no white cabin lighting to contrast with the glow, and nothing in the window that says plasma.
findings.realReference: Orion Artemis I, Soyuz and Crew Dragon entry footage from inside: the windows show streaming orange to pink-magenta glow with bright streaks and sparks, still coloured, not clipped; the glow pulses and washes over the window frames and the nearest surfaces only, while the cabin stays lit by its own white lamps and displays.
findings.likelyCause: kestrel.json lighting.plasmaLuminance 25000 with one colour [1.0, 0.42, 0.24] is added uniformly to every window's radiance (shaders.ts windowRadiance line 303) and spread over the cabin by the uniform bounce term; the lab scene has the floods off (labs/cockpit/main.ts SCENES.reentry lights: false), so it is the only light. The interior metering then exposes for the cabin and the 25000 cd/m^2 windows clip to white. The plasma itself is a lab stand-in.
findings.fixDirection: Meter interior views so that window highlights keep colour during entry (cabin goes darker, as in the footage); make the plasma light local and animated (falloff from the windows, 5-15 Hz flicker, colour from white-orange to pink) instead of a uniform tint; turn the floods on in the entry scene so white and orange light mix; re-shoot in the integration lab with the real plasma effect behind the glass.

findings.defect: The side hatch does not hold together. 1) Daylight leaks through a bright slit between the door and its frame along the upper-right edge (broken white line with bloom): the pressure hatch has a see-through gap. 2) Ten thin rods run in straight lines from the gearbox to the latches, several of them straight across the round window. 3) The latches are small black blocks that hover over the frame without engaging anything. 4) Handle and valve are flat pure-yellow and pure-red bars on black discs, and the seal ring's corners are visibly polygonal.
findings.realReference: The Apollo unified hatch and the Orion side hatch: the door seats on a continuous seal with no light path, the latches sit around the rim and are driven by a linkage that runs around the perimeter inside the rim from a gearbox with a pump handle, each latch is an over-centre hook on a striker, and the window is clear.
findings.likelyCause: src/render/cockpit/cabin/apertures.ts buildHatch(): line 222 `const doorLoop = offsetLoop(base, -0.004)` leaves a 4 mm annular gap that no geometry closes (the seal at lines 213-216 lies on the wall outside the opening), so the view goes through to whatever is behind; in the lab that is the back-face-culled stand-in hull, i.e. the sky. Lines 291-300 draw each rod as a straight tube from the gearbox to `local(face, u * 0.92, v * 0.92, 0.012)`, which crosses the window for every latch on the far side; latches are bare boxes (line 295).
findings.fixDirection: Close the gap with a seal surface from the opening outline to the door edge (and an outer door skin through the wall thickness) so no exterior is ever visible around the door. Replace the radial rods with a perimeter linkage inside the rim (bell crank at each latch, drive rod segments between them, one link to the gearbox), model latches as hooks over strikers on the frame, keep the window clear. Give handle and valve real shapes and worn paint, and raise the outline segment count at the corners.

findings.view: C:/dev/fable-space-game/out/screens/cockpit/closeup-switches.png (around the FINE switch); closeup-fdai.png (panel right of the instrument); night-displays-floods.png (left of every seven-segment readout and guarded switch)
findings.defect: The baked occlusion shows as stains. A soft black soot blob surrounds the FINE switch while its four identical neighbours have none; cloudy dark smears sit on the panel beside the FDAI; and a fan of dark 'speed lines' trails to the left of each readout window and each switch guard. They read as rendering faults, not as dirt, because they follow the mesh.
findings.realReference: Contact shadow around a toggle switch is a tight, even ring a few millimetres wide, the same at every switch; a flat panel is evenly lit between its fittings.
findings.likelyCause: The occlusion is stored per vertex (occlusion.ts, 16 bytes per vertex, transport.maxEdge 0.035 in kestrel.json) and interpolated across whatever triangles the panel was cut into: sliver triangles fanning from cut-outs give streaks, and a vertex that happens to sit under a lever gives a blob. shaders.ts line 774 then amplifies low occlusion into albedo: `grime = saturate(det.grime * mat.d.z * (1.6 - occ.ao - 0.6 * cavity))`, `albedo *= 1.0 - 0.45 * grime`.
findings.fixDirection: Bake occlusion for the console and wall panels into a texture (4-8 mm texels) or tessellate uniformly to 1 cm or finer around fittings and smooth the per-vertex result within each face. Keep small moving parts (levers, guards, knobs) out of the panel's occlusion beyond a contact radius. Take occ.ao out of the grime formula (use the texture mask and the modelled cavity only).

findings.defect: The console is a set of thin slabs floating in the cabin, and its hardware does not read. A slit between the upper and lower sections shows the bright wall behind it; from the seat the blankets, the tunnel ring and a flood are visible under and around the board, which has no visible support, back or cable feed. The lower panel is mostly empty black: eight switches and four rotaries on a board with room for sixty. Switch lever, nut and washer are the same near-black as the panel, so the row is black on black; the lever in its down position covers the lower legend (OFF and UP are cut at RCS, GEAR and LIGHTS). In the close-up the lower 40 percent of the frame is blank panel.
findings.realReference: Apollo main display console, Shuttle forward panels, Orion and Soyuz consoles: a deep structure bolted to the vehicle with visible mounts and cable bundles, panels butted with no see-through gaps, dense rows of bright nickel bat-handle switches with wicket guards between them, engraved white nomenclature above and below each switch inside group boxes, back-lit at night.
findings.likelyCause: src/render/cockpit/cabin/console.ts builds five independent boxes from kestrel.json console.sections (depth 0.16 and 0.07, the 'lower' section tilted -30 degrees from the others, nothing joining them or tying them to the shell). Switch metal uses 'steel' (metallic 1), which has nothing to reflect (first finding). Legends: console.ts lines 336-337 place the up and down texts at (0.0125, +/-0.0105) beside the lever, inside its swept area as seen from the seat. Content: two switch rows, four rotaries, four readouts in kestrel.json.
findings.fixDirection: Make the console one structure: close the joints with overlapping lips, add side cheeks, a back cover, mounts to the ring frames and cable bundles entering from behind. Put the position legends above and below the lever's throw, centred, clear of the lever. Fill the panels to real density (more switch groups with guards between them, group boxes and lines in the label atlas, breakers), and frame the switch close-up on a populated area. Bright metal for the levers follows from the cabin reflection.

findings.defect: The couches do not read as flight couches. Flat grey bars stick out from under the cushions at unrelated angles (left of the centre seat pad, lower right) like loose slats; cushions are large smooth navy pillows with a brushed-plastic streak texture and no seams, stitching or wrinkles; the harness is a slightly darker strip that cannot be told from the cushion, with a toy-like grey disc and red bar for a buckle; the hand controllers are black blobs on black boxes with white speckles on the edges; small blank grey plates sit on the seat sides; handle and buttons are saturated yellow and red.
findings.realReference: Apollo and Orion crew couches: a tubular or machined frame with a clear load path to the attenuator struts, foot pans and restraints, fabric-covered pads with stitched seams, piping and creases, wide webbing straps with adjusters, stitching and a metal rotary buckle, grips with moulded texture and worn, satin surfaces.
findings.likelyCause: src/render/cockpit/cabin/couches.ts: pans and rails are flat boxes and tubes placed per seat segment (lines 157-201) whose ends overshoot the pads when thighDeg and kneeDeg fold the leg section (kestrel.json couches.seats); cushion material 'cushion' uses the generic 'weave' layer at one scale; the harness (line 265 on) is FLAG_OVERLAY webbing in nearly the cushion's colour (webbing [0.05, 0.06, 0.09] against cushion [0.085, 0.092, 0.11]); wear dots as in the first finding.
findings.fixDirection: Rebuild the frame as one connected structure (side beams, hinged seat and leg pans that end at the pad outline, struts to hard points), give pads stitched panel seams and soft wrinkles in geometry, make the harness a contrasting webbing (grey or tan) with modelled adjusters, stitching and a metal buckle, and tone the primary colours down to worn paint and anodise. Check the fold of each seat so no part pokes through or past another.

findings.defect: The wall of every window well (the cut through the hull seen through the glass) is covered in a coarse worm-like stipple, strongest in the hatch window and in the moon view, where it frames the whole view like a halftone print.
findings.realReference: A window well is smooth painted or anodised metal with a clean shadow edge and perhaps a sealant bead; seen from 30 cm it has no grain.
findings.likelyCause: The well faces belong to the exterior (here labs/cockpit/hull.ts lines 65-79, drawn by the core mesh system) and take their sun from the core's cascades, whose rotated-noise PCF leaves grain at this range and grazing incidence: the fault the cockpit removed from its own surfaces by leaving the cascades (hand-off deviation 1, request cockpit-4). The real exterior's wells will be lit the same way, so this will remain in the game.
findings.fixDirection: Have the cockpit own what is seen through its glass at arm's length: extend the bezel tunnel outward through the wall thickness to the outer mould line as a cockpit-drawn well liner lit by the analytic aperture term (it hides the exterior's well from inside), or request a noise-free near filter from the core for surfaces within about 1 m of an interior camera. Verify in the integration lab with the real exterior.

findings.defect: Window and bezel corners are polygons. Where a window fills the frame the corner of the opening is four or five straight segments, and the outer corners of every bezel are plain 45 degree chamfers (octagonal frames in the reentry and pad views).
findings.realReference: Window frames are machined with true radii; the highlight runs around the corner without a kink.
findings.likelyCause: src/render/cockpit/mould.ts roundedRectOutline() (line 131) spaces its points evenly along the perimeter, and src/render/cockpit/cabin/apertures.ts asks for 64 points per window (line 153) and 72 for the hatch (line 208): two to five points land on each corner arc. offsetLoop() then offsets those few points for the bezel rings.
findings.fixDirection: Sample outlines by curvature: at least 12-16 segments per corner arc at lod0 and only as many as needed on the straights (the count per loop must stay equal across the rings built from it). The geometry test that compares frames with the shared opening should sample the corners.

findings.view: C:/dev/fable-space-game/out/screens/cockpit/pad-noon-forward-window.png (left of each window); reentry-plasma.png; hatch-mechanism.png (two pale squares on the door and frame); look-back-couches-hatch.png (grey plates on the seat sides)
findings.defect: Blank squares float in the cabin. Pale 5 cm squares with visible thickness hover a couple of centimetres off the blankets beside the windows, tilted against the wall like sticky notes, and more sit on the hatch and seats. With no texture readable they look like missing placards.
findings.realReference: Velcro in a crewed cabin is small (2-3 cm) squares and strips lying flush, usually in rows or grids, blue, tan or white with a visibly fuzzy pile; nothing hovers.
findings.likelyCause: src/render/cockpit/cabin/fixtures.ts lines 196-200: nine patches placed with `wallFrame(ctx, az, y, plateInset(ctx, az, y, 0.05, 0.05, 0.002) + 0.023)`, i.e. 23 mm inside the wall plane as a flat box, while the blanket under them is curved and only 16 mm thick; the 'velcro' detail layer is invisible at this size.
findings.fixDirection: Seat each patch on the surface under it (project onto the blanket or panel and follow its curvature, 1 mm proud), shrink to 25 mm, place in rows and grids where crews put them, and give hook and loop pile a readable normal and colour. Remove any plate that carries no label.

findings.defect: The attitude instrument is a game navball in a plain black square. The ball is the orange and blue sphere with a cartoon yellow aircraft marker; there are no rate or error needles, no scales beyond a painted tick ring, the four 'screws' are flat grey discs with no slot or recess, and nothing suggests a glass face: no reflection, no highlight, no depth between glass and ball.
findings.realReference: The Apollo FDAI: a ball in black, white and grey with fine engraved graduations and red gimbal-lock zones behind a domed glass that shows reflections, three rate needles on outer scales, three yellow error needles across the face, a roll index, and a bezel with recessed screws.
findings.likelyCause: src/render/cockpit/shaders.ts BALL_WGSL shades the shared 'ui.navball' image as a diffuse dome with a fixed roughness and no cover glass in front of it; console.ts builds the housing as a box with a printed ring label ('#ROLL' in atlas.ts) and cylinders for screws. The ball artwork comes from the HUD's navball renderer.
findings.fixDirection: Add a domed cover glass over the instrument in the glass pass (it will pick up the cabin reflection), set the ball back behind it with a shadowed gap, model the bezel ring, recessed slotted screws and the needles (rate and error needles can be driven from the snapshot's rates and SAS error), and ask the UI package for an instrument-grade ball texture option (fine graduations, muted colours) for the physical instrument.

findings.view: C:/dev/fable-space-game/out/screens/cockpit/night-displays-floods.png (caution and warning panel, upper right of the console); leo-sun-patch-console.png; C:/dev/fable-space-game/out/screens/integration/budget-leo-cockpit.png
findings.defect: Annunciator legends come in two sizes. One-word legends (MAINS, DROGUES) are drawn about twice as tall and heavier than the two-word ones, so they look lit or more important while unlit; the small ones are an unreadable blur from the seat.
findings.realReference: A caution and warning matrix uses one cap height and one stroke weight in every cell; an unlit legend is equally faint everywhere.
findings.likelyCause: src/render/cockpit/atlas.ts lines 63-66: the font size is `(h / rows.length) * 0.78`, so a legend that is not split into two rows gets double the size, and `fillText(..., maxWidth)` then squeezes it.
findings.fixDirection: Use one cap height for all lens legends (the two-row size), centre single-row legends vertically, and raise unlit legend contrast slightly so the panel reads from the seat.

findings.defect: Everything inside the sun patch is one flat white: the black anodised MFD bezel becomes white plastic, the panel a white cut-out. There is no glare or bloom around the patch and the dark panel right beside it stays black.
findings.realReference: In Apollo and ISS interior photographs a sun patch is overexposed but still shows the surface (texture, screw heads, colour at the edges), it flares softly into its surroundings, and it visibly lifts the light on everything facing it.
findings.likelyCause: Exposure follows the dim cabin, so a sunlit surface of albedo 0.03-0.085 is five stops over and clips with a hard shoulder; whatever bloom the core applies does not show at this size, and the bounce from the patch reaches only non-coplanar surfaces.
findings.fixDirection: Let interior metering weigh the sun patch (a stop or so darker when a patch is in view), check the tone curve's shoulder keeps texture up to about +4 EV, and confirm the bloom threshold lets a clipped patch flare.

findings.defect: MFD finish: the bezel's soft keys are blank blocks with no legends and do not line up with the page tabs on the screen; the flight page leaves its lower third empty and its attitude graphic is a two-colour disc; the third display's text is too small to read from the seat at 1600 x 900.
findings.realReference: Glass-cockpit displays (Orion, Dragon, Shuttle MEDS): every bezel key has an on-screen label beside it, pages are laid out to the full screen, and text is sized for the seat distance.
findings.likelyCause: src/render/cockpit/cabin/console.ts places five keys per side at fixed spacing unrelated to the painter's layout; page content comes from the UI package's MfdPainter.
findings.fixDirection: Align the key positions with the painter's soft-key label slots (or have the painter draw labels at the key positions the layout file gives), and pass the layout issues to the flight-ui owner. Also re-run the perf spec so perf-1440p-leo-seat.png is current; it is the only screenshot in the folder not regenerated on 11 Nov.
